reconcile.connective: Harmonizers across the tradition read Hebrews 7:3 as a claim about Melchizedek's unrecorded priestly genealogy, not a denial that he had natural parents or Adamic descent.

discrepancy.empty_note: No critic of record presses Hebrews 7:3 against universal Adamic descent; the skeptical lists treat it as a genealogy puzzle, and named critics (e.g., Paine) target the Gospel genealogies of Jesus, not this verse. Naming a skeptic here would strawman.

excerpts.excerpt_text: for no doubt, as he was a mere man, he had a father, and a mother, and a natural lineage and descent; but of these no mention is made in Scripture, and therefore said to be without them
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies the literal reading: Melchizedek did have natural parents and descent (so no breach of universal Adamic descent); 'without father/mother' only means Scripture is silent about them.

excerpts.excerpt_text: In this way both Christ and Melchisedec were without father and without mother; i.e. were not descended from the original Jewish sacerdotal stock.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reframes the phrase as priestly-stock language, not biological; resolves the apparent conflict with universal natural descent.

excerpts.excerpt_text: That we have no record of Melchizedek's father or mother or any of his ancestors is significant in light of the ancestral requirement upon which the Levitical priesthood was based.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Modern voice making the same harmonizing move: the verse concerns absence of genealogical record relative to priestly qualification, not literal parentlessness.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Hebrews 7:3
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage at length, marshaling Owen, Suidas, Seneca, Livy, and Horace to argue that 'without father, without mother, without descent' means a person whose pedigree is nowhere recorded, not one who literally had no parents or natural descent. Used as the PD anchor because Haley's specific coverage of Hebrews 7:3 could not be confirmed; Clarke is a harmonizing commentator already surfaced on this row, keyed directly to the verse.
